result: The paperweight sits on my desk, a glass hemisphere with a tiny bubble at its center. It is not a treasure, nor an heirloom. It is simply a thing that holds the day's receipts and unanswered mail. But when the light strikes it just so, the bubble catches the sun and becomes a perfect bead of fire, and the whole object hums with a hidden life. In that moment I am reminded that the world is full of such quiet miracles, waiting for some incidental beam to reveal them. We walk through our days in haste, seeing what we expect to see, blind to the small astonishments that surround us—the grain of wood on a chair, the comma-shaped crack on a windowpane, the way a curtain folds in a draft. The paperweight is my teacher. It asks nothing of me except attention. And attention, perhaps, is the only true gift we can give to anything. In giving it, we become less alone. The universe, or at least the one that fits inside our sight, begins to unfold in answer to our looking. I have never known its maker. I do not know how it came to be mine. Yet it has taught me patience, and it has taught me that even the most ordinary object, held up to the light, can become a doorway. It is enough to sit here and watch. The world asks nothing more. The bubble at its center is, in miniature, the eye of the world.
